payload.body_text:
An agent can pass every evaluation and still become unsafe on Tuesday.

Doctrine Half-Life is how long the premises governing its actions remain valid, current, and understood before the world—or the organization—moves on.

That clock should bound permission.

If a customer-facing agent was authorized under a pricing doctrine expected to hold for 30 days, its permission should not survive for 90. The agent may still execute perfectly. That is the danger: it can faithfully apply a stale map at machine speed.

Passing an evaluation proves performance under a set of premises. It does not make those premises permanent. Every autonomous permission should expire no later than the doctrine that justified it.

novel_idea.topic_thesis: Every autonomous permission should expire no later than the doctrine that justified it.
novel_idea.angle: Introduce Doctrine Half-Life as the missing clock in agent governance: permissions should be time-bounded by how long their governing premises are expected to remain valid, not granted indefinitely because an agent once passed evaluation.
novel_idea.hook: An agent can pass every alignment test on Monday and become dangerous by Friday without changing at all.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Autonomous permissions are usually treated as durable once an agent demonstrates capability and contextual alignment. But the source distinguishes agent fidelity from doctrine validity: an agent can remain perfectly faithful while the organization’s diagnosis, tradeoffs, or commitments become stale. As doctrine ages, persistent permissions turn yesterday’s correct instructions into today’s confidently executed error. Therefore the duration of autonomy should be bounded by Doctrine Half-Life, with reauthorization requiring current doctrine, evaluations, and reality feedback. The operator decision is temporal: do not merely decide how much an agent may do; decide how long that authority remains valid before it must be renewed or reduced.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest prior post argues that false doctrine can produce Coherent Wrongness when agents execute it faithfully without sufficient reality feedback. This argument identifies a different causal mechanism and operator decision: doctrine can begin valid and become dangerous through ordinary aging, even when the agent, evaluations, and execution remain unchanged. The substantive addition is to bind permission duration to Doctrine Half-Life, making expiration and reauthorization part of autonomy design rather than relying only on initial alignment or eventual contradiction.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source defines Doctrine Half-Life as how long doctrine remains valid, current, and understood before drift or world change makes it stale. It states that bounded agents require current doctrine, permissions, evaluations, stop conditions, and feedback paths; asks who is accountable when doctrine ages but an agent keeps acting; and warns that stale doctrine can regulate confidently from a false model. The Minimum Viable Coherence Program also ties higher permission levels to mature doctrine, evaluations, and Actor feedback.

payload.topic_thesis: A leader should not frame candor as a gift exchange unless they are willing to become indebted to the subordinate who tells an uncontrollable truth.

payload.hook: Candor can invert a hierarchy. That is why some leaders punish it.
payload.body_text:
Candor can invert a hierarchy. That is why some leaders punish it.

“The subordinate becomes the creditor; the leader becomes the debtor.”

Not Marcel Mauss caught the part of the gift metaphor most leaders would rather ignore.

A leader offers protected time, hospitality, attention. Then a junior person names the false premise behind the strategy—and everyone in the room knows it is true. The employee has now given the greater gift. Rank remains on paper, but the moral debt runs upward.

Many organizations permit criticism only while it leaves status intact. When candor becomes uncontrollable—when it obligates the leader to change, concede, or repay—the “safe space” suddenly develops consequences.

If you frame candor as a gift, you must accept the debt it creates. If you cannot let a subordinate’s truth put you in their debt, do not call the meeting safe.

novel_idea.topic_thesis: A leader should not frame candor as a gift exchange unless they are willing to become indebted to the subordinate who tells an uncontrollable truth.
novel_idea.angle: Reverse the hospitality argument: the danger is not that employees will fail to reciprocate, but that their candor may become the greater gift, invert the hierarchy, and provoke retaliation from a leader unwilling to accept the debt.
novel_idea.hook: The dangerous moment in a candor session is when the employee gives more than the leader can repay.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Protected time and hospitality do not make candor safe by themselves. In gift logic, receiving creates obligation, and the greater gift can establish superiority. If a subordinate returns the leader’s hospitality with a truth potent enough to force structural change, the subordinate becomes the creditor and the leader the debtor. A leader who expected manageable feedback may answer that inversion with punishment. The operator test is therefore not whether leadership made the session feel generous, but whether leadership has precommitted to accept a response whose value and consequences it cannot control—and to change the system accordingly.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest prior post argues that expensive hospitality creates a reciprocal obligation to return candor. This argument identifies the opposite causal mechanism and boundary: candor itself may become the greater gift, invert the hierarchy, and create a debt leadership resists through retaliation. The new operator decision is to test whether leaders can surrender control over the return gift, not merely whether they can host generously.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The mailbag letter from Not Marcel Mauss states that gifts carry burden and superiority; if a subordinate offers a truth leadership cannot match or metabolize, the subordinate becomes the creditor and the leader the debtor. It warns that calling a meeting a gift does not remove hierarchy and that the giver must accept a response whose value and consequences they do not control.
